L2-S2.explanation: A contusion is a bruise without a break in the skin or mucosa, with subcutaneous or submucosal haemorrhage.

L11-S2.explanation: A contusion is a bruise without a break in the skin or mucosa, with subcutaneous or submucosal haemorrhage.

L2-S3.explanation: Vital pulp therapy (partial pulpotomy) and pulp space revascularisation/regenerative endodontics allow continued root development; MTA apexification, first-stage endodontics and gutta-percha obturation do not.
L2-S3.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 4

L11-S3.explanation: Vital pulp therapy (partial pulpotomy) and pulp space revascularisation/regenerative endodontics allow continued root development; MTA apexification, first-stage endodontics and gutta-percha obturation do not.
L11-S3.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 4

L2-S4.explanation: Treatment aims to protect the pulp and restore function and aesthetics: tooth fragment reattachment, composite resin restoration or a temporary glass ionomer restoration.
L2-S4.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 3 (enamel-dentine fracture)

L11-S4.explanation: Treatment aims to protect the pulp and restore function and aesthetics: tooth fragment reattachment, composite resin restoration or a temporary glass ionomer restoration.
L11-S4.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 3 (enamel-dentine fracture)

L2-S5.explanation: Replacement resorption (ankylosis) cannot be arrested or repaired.

L11-S5.explanation: Replacement resorption (ankylosis) cannot be arrested or repaired.

L2-S6.explanation: The combination of bacteria in the root canal (pulp necrosis) AND cemental/PDL damage on the external root surface results in external inflammatory root resorption.

L11-S6.explanation: The combination of bacteria in the root canal (pulp necrosis) AND cemental/PDL damage on the external root surface results in external inflammatory root resorption.

L2-S7.explanation: Replanted permanent teeth should be stabilised for 2 weeks with a passive, flexible splint (4 weeks only if there is an associated alveolar or jaw-bone fracture).
L2-S7.source: IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 8 (Stabilization of replanted teeth)

L11-S7.explanation: Replanted permanent teeth should be stabilised for 2 weeks with a passive, flexible splint (4 weeks only if there is an associated alveolar or jaw-bone fracture).
L11-S7.source: IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 8 (Stabilization of replanted teeth)

L2-S8.explanation: Apexification is a method to induce a calcified barrier in a root with an open apex in teeth with necrotic pulps.

L11-S8.explanation: Apexification is a method to induce a calcified barrier in a root with an open apex in teeth with necrotic pulps.

L2-S9.explanation: Replacement resorption (ankylosis) presents with reduced mobility and a high (metallic) percussion tone; it is the expected outcome after long extra-oral time (>60 min).
L2-S9.source: IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 11.3

L11-S9.explanation: Replacement resorption (ankylosis) presents with reduced mobility and a high (metallic) percussion tone; it is the expected outcome after long extra-oral time (>60 min).
L11-S9.source: IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 11.3

L2-S10.explanation: The fracture extends below the gingival margin palatally (crown-root fracture) and the pulp is exposed, so this is a complicated crown-root fracture.
L2-S10.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 6

L11-S10.explanation: The fracture extends below the gingival margin palatally (crown-root fracture) and the pulp is exposed, so this is a complicated crown-root fracture.
L11-S10.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 6

L2-S11.explanation: Crown fractures without luxation never need a splint. In subluxation, normally no treatment is needed; a passive flexible splint for up to 2 weeks is used only if there is excessive mobility or tenderness on biting.
L2-S11.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Tables 2–4 and 10

L11-S11.explanation: Crown fractures without luxation never need a splint. In subluxation, normally no treatment is needed; a passive flexible splint for up to 2 weeks is used only if there is excessive mobility or tenderness on biting.
L11-S11.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Tables 2–4 and 10

L2-S12.explanation: This is an enamel-dentine-pulp (complicated crown) fracture in an immature tooth seen early; partial (Cvek) pulpotomy preserves the pulp and promotes further root development. Direct pulp capping is also acceptable for a pinpoint exposure treated immediately (IADT: partial pulpotomy or pulp capping); among the options given, partial pulpotomy is the best choice.
L2-S12.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 4

L11-S12.explanation: This is an enamel-dentine-pulp (complicated crown) fracture in an immature tooth seen early; partial (Cvek) pulpotomy preserves the pulp and promotes further root development. Direct pulp capping is also acceptable for a pinpoint exposure treated immediately (IADT: partial pulpotomy or pulp capping); among the options given, partial pulpotomy is the best choice.
L11-S12.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 4

L2-S13.explanation: Sensibility tests indirectly assess the pulp by its neural response to a stimulus, not pulp vitality (blood supply).
L2-S13.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), section 5.1 (Sensibility tests)

L11-S13.explanation: Sensibility tests indirectly assess the pulp by its neural response to a stimulus, not pulp vitality (blood supply).
L11-S13.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), section 5.1 (Sensibility tests)

L2-S14.explanation: The root outline and PDL space are being lost and the root is replaced by bone (direct union of bone and root), typical of replacement resorption after avulsion.
L2-S14.source: IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 11.3

L11-S14.explanation: The root outline and PDL space are being lost and the root is replaced by bone (direct union of bone and root), typical of replacement resorption after avulsion.
L11-S14.source: IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 11.3

L2-S15.explanation: An increased overjet with the lower lip trapped behind the upper incisors (incompetent lips) increases the risk of dental trauma.

L11-S15.explanation: An increased overjet with the lower lip trapped behind the upper incisors (incompetent lips) increases the risk of dental trauma.

L2-S16.explanation: A functional splint should include at least one uninjured tooth on either side of the injured tooth: 12-11-21.

L11-S16.explanation: A functional splint should include at least one uninjured tooth on either side of the injured tooth: 12-11-21.

L2-S17.explanation: The MEBDTI records the FDI tooth code followed by five digits (crown fracture, root fracture, luxation injury, maturity/shape of apex, alveolar process fracture) plus superscript soft tissue injury codes. Universal numbering and aetiology are not part of the index.

L11-S17.explanation: The MEBDTI records the FDI tooth code followed by five digits (crown fracture, root fracture, luxation injury, maturity/shape of apex, alveolar process fracture) plus superscript soft tissue injury codes. Universal numbering and aetiology are not part of the index.

L2-S18.explanation: Upper right central incisor (11): enamel-dentine fracture (2), no root fracture (0), no luxation (N), immature apex (i), no alveolar fracture (-); upper lip laceration (2) and contusion (3).

L11-S18.explanation: Upper right central incisor (11): enamel-dentine fracture (2), no root fracture (0), no luxation (N), immature apex (i), no alveolar fracture (-); upper lip laceration (2) and contusion (3).

L2-S19.explanation: 11: no crown or root fracture, lateral luxation, immature apex, alveolar fracture [(11) 00Li+]; 21: enamel-dentine fracture, immature apex, no luxation [(21) 20Ni-]; intra-oral (gingival) laceration = 6.

L11-S19.explanation: 11: no crown or root fracture, lateral luxation, immature apex, alveolar fracture [(11) 00Li+]; 21: enamel-dentine fracture, immature apex, no luxation [(21) 20Ni-]; intra-oral (gingival) laceration = 6.

L3-S21.explanation: Image A shows abrasions (superficial scraping of the skin) of the chin and lip; images B and C show wounds that break through the mucosa/lip (lacerations).

L3-S22.explanation: A fracture confined to enamel and dentine with loss of tooth structure, without visible pulp exposure.

L3-S23.explanation: A fracture confined to the enamel with loss of tooth structure (small chip of the incisal corner of 11).

L3-S24.explanation: A fracture involving enamel and dentine with loss of tooth structure and exposure of the pulp (the red pulp exposure point is visible).

L3-S25.explanation: Necrotic pulp (negative sensibility tests) plus PDL damage after avulsion, with radiolucent areas along the root a month after replantation, indicates external inflammatory root resorption.

L3-S26.explanation: The tooth is in infra-occlusion relative to the adjacent teeth and the root is being replaced by bone, the signs of replacement resorption (ankylosis) in a growing child.

L3-S27.explanation: Root fracture: involves dentine, cementum and the pulp. Intrusive luxation: displacement of the tooth into the alveolar bone. Subluxation: injury to the supporting structures with abnormal loosening but no displacement. Enamel-dentine fracture: loss of enamel and dentine without pulp involvement.
L3-S27.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Tables 2, 7, 9, 13

explanations: False - the 2nd digit describes root fractures; luxation injuries are the 3rd digit.
True - the 5th digit (+/-) records the presence or absence of an alveolar process fracture.
True - the 2nd digit records root fractures (0 none, 1 apical, 2 middle, 3 cervical third).
False - the index uses the FDI tooth code, not Palmer notation.
True - the 4th digit records maturity and shape of the apex (i, m, r).
True - the 1st digit records crown fractures (0-5).

L4-S9.explanation: The left central incisor is tooth 21 in FDI notation, so the correct code is (21)00Ei- (not 11).
explanations: The left central incisor is tooth 21 in FDI notation, so the correct code is (21)00Ei- (not 11).

This statement is correct.

This statement is correct.

Left central incisor with crown facture with pulp exposure and lateral luxation with alveolar process fracture will get the code: (21)30Lm+
explanations:
This statement is correct.

Left central incisor with crown facture with pulp exposure and lateral luxation with alveolar process fracture will get the code: (21)30Lm+

L4-S12.explanation:
This statement is correct.

Lateral incisor with crown fracture in dentin without pulp exposure and root fracture in apical third of the root with mature apex (12)21Nm-

L5-S28.explanation: Pulp sensibility testing is not recommended in primary teeth (unreliable in young children).
L5-S28.source: IADT 2020 Primary Dentition (Day et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:343-359), section 1.5 ('Pulp sensibility tests are unreliable in primary teeth and are therefore not recommended')

L5-S29.explanation: False - a temporary loss of sensibility is a frequent finding during post-traumatic pulp healing and is not conclusive for pulp necrosis; endodontic treatment should not be started solely on the basis of no response to sensibility testing.
L5-S29.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), section 5.1 and Table 11 (extrusive luxation, favourable outcomes)
explanations: False - a temporary loss of sensibility is a frequent finding during post-traumatic pulp healing and is not conclusive for pulp necrosis; endodontic treatment should not be started solely on the basis of no response to sensibility testing.

L5-S30.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 12 (lateral luxation: 'Likely to have no response to pulp sensibility tests')
explanations: True - young patients may not understand the test or cooperate, so results can be inconclusive.
True - a negative response is common after lateral luxation (temporary loss of sensibility during pulp healing).
False - the EPT stimulates intact myelinated A-delta fibres, not C fibres.

L6-S7.explanation: Avulsion: 2 weeks. Subluxation: a splint for up to 2 weeks only if there is excessive mobility or tenderness on biting. Root fracture: 4 weeks, up to 4 months if the fracture is cervical.
L6-S7.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Tables 7 and 10; IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 8

L6-S8.explanation: Extrusive luxation: stabilise the tooth for 2 weeks using a passive and flexible splint.
L6-S8.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 11 (extrusive luxation)

L6-S9.explanation: When surgical repositioning of an intruded tooth is indicated, the tooth should be splinted with a passive and flexible splint for 4 weeks.
L6-S9.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 13 (intrusive luxation)

L6-S10.explanation: The splint should include at least one uninjured tooth on either side of the injured tooth: 11-21-22.

L7-S14.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Tables 2 and 3
explanations: False - the exposed dentine should be covered at the emergency visit (fragment reattachment, composite or temporary glass ionomer); revascularisation is not relevant to an enamel-dentine fracture.
False - clinical and radiographic evaluations are needed after 6-8 weeks and after 1 year.
True - if the fragment is missing and there are soft tissue injuries, radiographs of the lip and/or cheek are indicated to search for tooth fragments and/or foreign materials.
True - treatment consists primarily of protecting the pulp from external insults, e.g. covering the dentine to prevent bacterial invasion into the dentinal tubules.
False - a soft tissue radiograph is indicated only when the fragment is missing AND there are soft tissue injuries.

False - if the exposed dentine is within 0.5 mm of the pulp (pink but no bleeding), a calcium hydroxide lining is placed and covered (e.g. with glass ionomer); partial pulpotomy is for pulp exposures.
True - if there is an associated luxation, root fracture or suspicion of an associated luxation injury, the luxation follow-up regimen prevails.
True - minor enamel fractures can be managed without a restoration (no treatment or smoothing/polishing of sharp edges).

L7-S15.explanation:
According to the IADT 2020 guidelines, clinical and radiographic evaluations are necessary:
- After 6-8 weeks
- After 1 year
L7-S15.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 2

L7-S16.explanation: IADT: fragment reattachment, smoothing of sharp edges or composite resin restoration. A very small enamel chip may simply be monitored.
L7-S16.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 2 (enamel fracture)

L8-S9.explanation: Complicated crown fractures: clinical and radiographic evaluations after 6-8 weeks, 3 months, 6 months and 1 year (12 months).
L8-S9.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 4

L8-S11.explanation: Partial (Cvek) pulpotomy has a high success rate in teeth with open apices but can also be used in teeth with closed apices.
L8-S11.source: IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 4

L9-S18.source: IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 2 (First aid at the place of accident); signs of brain injury (dizziness, disorientation) require hospital referral
explanations: False - a tooth wrapped in a tissue dries out. If it cannot be replanted, place it as soon as possible in a storage medium (milk, HBSS, saliva or saline).
True - dizziness or disorientation may indicate a head injury; the child needs medical (hospital) assessment first.
False - avoid touching the root. If the tooth is dirty, rinse it gently in milk, saline or the patient's saliva.
False - pick the tooth up by the crown, but place it in a storage medium (milk, HBSS, saliva or saline) rather than a dry plastic bag.
False - immediate replantation at the place of the accident is the best treatment; the parent should be encouraged to replant the tooth.
True - if the tooth is dirty, rinse it gently in milk, saline or the patient's saliva and replant it.

L9-S19.explanation: In descending order of preference, milk, HBSS, saliva (after spitting into a glass for instance), or saline are suitable and convenient storage mediums. Although water is a poor medium, it is better than leaving the tooth to air-dry.
L9-S19.source: IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 2, point 6

L9-S20.explanation: The tooth has been replanted immediately or within a very short time (about 15 minutes) at the place of accident.
L9-S20.source: IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 3

L9-S21.explanation: The PDL cells may be viable but compromised. The tooth has been kept in a storage medium (eg, milk, HBSS (Save-a-Tooth or similar product), saliva, or saline, and the total extra-oral dry time has been <60 minutes).
L9-S21.source: IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 3

L9-S22.explanation: The PDL cells are likely to be non-viable. The total extra-oral dry time has been more than 60 minutes, regardless of the tooth having been stored in a medium or not. Note: IADT also states that after about 30 minutes of dry time most PDL cells are no longer viable; the 60-minute cut-off is the one used for treatment decisions.
L9-S22.source: IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 3

L9-S24.explanation: In avulsed teeth with a closed apex the pulp should be removed and root canal treatment initiated within 2 weeks after replantation; in open-apex teeth root canal treatment is avoided unless pulp necrosis is diagnosed, because revascularisation may occur.
L9-S24.source: IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 10 (Endodontic considerations)
